title: New Zealand Moves to Ban Social Media for Children Under 16 With Steep Fines
excerpt: The proposed legislation would require platforms to verify users' ages and could impose fines of up to 10% of global revenue for non-compliance, joining a growing international movement.
body:
• New Zealand's coalition government will introduce a bill in Parliament on Monday banning children under 16 from using social media platforms.
  • Non-compliant platforms face fines of up to 10% of their global revenue — among the steepest penalties proposed worldwide.
  • The bill requires age verification using existing account data, facial recognition technology, and digital identity documents.
  • New Zealand joins Australia, France, Denmark, Malaysia, and others in a growing international push to restrict children's access to social media.

Government Tables Landmark Bill

New Zealand's conservative coalition government will introduce legislation in Parliament on Monday seeking to ban children under 16 from using social media, proposing some of the most aggressive penalties yet seen in the global push to protect minors online.

The bill would require social media platforms to take "reasonable steps" to verify users' ages, including through existing account information, facial recognition technology, and digital identity documents. Platforms that fail to comply could face fines of up to 10% of their global revenue — a penalty structure that could translate to billions of dollars for major companies.

"We simply cannot accept the harm being done to a generation of New Zealand children. Social media is exposing them to harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not equipped to deal with and it's affecting their family life, mental health, sleep, and education."

— Christopher Luxon, Prime Minister of New Zealand

From Committee Report to Legislation

The bill represents the culmination of more than a year of parliamentary scrutiny. A member's bill submitted in May 2025 by National Party lawmaker Catherine Wedd originally proposed the ban with fines of up to NZ$2 million. The government has significantly escalated the penalties in the new legislation.

Parliament's Education and Workforce Select Committee published a final report earlier this year recommending the ban and creation of a national online safety regulator. The committee acknowledged that New Zealand is too small to regulate offshore tech companies alone and urged alignment with Australia, the European Union, and the United Kingdom for maximum leverage.

Prime Minister Luxon has pointed to the success of New Zealand's existing smartphone ban in schools, citing "increased student engagement and improved learning outcomes" as evidence that regulating children's access to technology works.

Part of a Global Wave

New Zealand's proposed legislation joins an accelerating international movement. Australia passed the world's first teen social media ban in 2024, while Denmark has banned social media for children under 15. Malaysia began barring those under 16 from registering social media accounts in June 2026. France's parliament approved a similar ban for under-15s, though it was blocked by the country's top court on free expression grounds in August.

India's chief economic adviser has called for age restrictions, describing platforms as "predatory" in how they keep users engaged. The tourist state of Goa has weighed restrictions modeled on Australia's approach.

Critics Raise Privacy and Enforcement Concerns

Not everyone supports the approach. Civil liberties organization PILLAR has warned the bill would create "serious privacy risks" through age verification requirements and could restrict online freedom for all New Zealanders, not just children.

"Aligning with international efforts may sound responsible, but it is lazy policymaking," PILLAR Executive Director Nathan Seiuli said.

The bill's coalition partners have not publicly confirmed whether they will support the legislation. Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has argued that such bans "can be easily circumvented" and risk transferring responsibility to families rather than holding platforms accountable.

If passed, the bill would make New Zealand one of a growing list of countries attempting to draw a regulatory line between children and the social media platforms that have become central to modern communication.
nri_angle: The global trend toward social media age restrictions is relevant to Indian-American parents navigating digital safety for their children, and India's own discussions about implementing similar measures.
